papers.what_it_is: Experimental paper proposing a variational quantum classifier and a quantum kernel estimator that use a quantum state space as the feature space, run on two qubits of an IBM superconducting processor.

assertions.value: The paper proposes two classifiers (a quantum variational classifier and a quantum kernel estimator) that use a quantum feature map, and runs both on a superconducting processor, using two qubits and artificial data built to be separable by the feature map. For the quantum kernel estimator, the third data set averaged 94.75% test success.
quotes: Here, we propose and experimentally implement two novel methods on a superconducting processor.
whereas Set III averages a success of 94.75%. For more details see the supplementary information.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reported hardware results, but on a 2-qubit toy problem with data generated to be perfectly classifiable by the same feature map.

assertions.value: The paper states that a quantum advantage for either method requires a kernel that cannot be estimated classically, and conjectures (without proof) that kernels built from circuits with two basis changes and diagonal gates, up to additive error, are hard to evaluate classically.
assertions.anchor: Introduction p. 2; Quantum feature map p. 2
quotes: A necessary condition to obtain a quantum advantage, in either of the two approaches, is that the kernel cannot be estimated classically.
We conjecture that the evaluation of inner products generated from circuits with two basis changes and diagonal gates up to additive error to be hard
assertions.certainty_reason: Necessary-condition argument is sound, but the hardness of the specific feature map is explicitly a conjecture.

assertions.value: The paper shows by expansion in a Pauli matrix basis that the variational circuit followed by a binary measurement is a separating hyperplane in quantum state space, so the classifier has the standard SVM form and a kernel method can find the optimal weights.
assertions.anchor: A path to quantum advantage, p. 4
quotes: The variational circuit W followed by a binary measurement can be understood as a separating hyperplane in quantum state space.
assertions.certainty_reason: Short derivation in the main text, not a formal theorem; quote supports the hyperplane equivalence only.

assertions.value: The conclusion leaves a provable quantum advantage for this technique as future work, so the paper itself does not demonstrate one. The experiment was designed to test hardware implementability, not advantage on real data.
quotes: suitable feature maps for this technique with provable quantum advantages while providing
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the authors as an open goal; the paper provides no advantage proof.

papers.what_it_is: Early survey of quantum machine learning (2014) organized by classical method: nearest neighbour, SVM, clustering, neural networks, decision trees, Bayesian methods and hidden Markov models.

assertions.value: The survey finds two main approaches to quantum machine learning, and says algorithmic complexity improvements are mostly proposed for nearest neighbour, kernel and clustering methods, where expensive distance calculations are sped up by quantum computation.
quotes: In summary, there are two main approaches to quantum machine learning.
This is dominantly true for nearest neighbour, kernel and clustering methods in which expensive distance calculations are sped up by quantum computation.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' own summary of the surveyed literature as of 2014; no new result.

assertions.value: As of 2014 the survey reports that neural networks and decision trees lacked a convincing quantum version and that a quantum theory of learning was still outstanding.
quotes: Neural networks and decision trees are still waiting for a convincing quantum version, although especially the former has been
As previously remarked, a quantum theory of learning is yet outstanding.
assertions.certainty_reason: Accurate description of 2014 state, but dated: later work (variational QNNs) changed this.

assertions.value: The survey reports the quantum SVM speedup as a claim by Rebentrost, Mohseni and Lloyd that inner products are faster on a quantum computer, notes the input state is built with a Quantum Random Access Memory oracle, and says another proposal (quantum k-median clustering) depends on an oracle left undescribed, so its resource cost is open.
assertions.anchor: Sec. 3.2 and footnote 6, p. 9-10; Sec. 3.3, p. 10
quotes: Rebentrost, Mohseni and Lloyd [12] claim that in general, the evaluation of an inner product can be done faster on a quantum computer.
The initial state can be constructed by using a Quantum Random Access Memory oracle described in [44], accessing a
oracle is not described in detail, and their quantum machine learning proposal largely depends on how and with what resources it can be implemented.
assertions.certainty_reason: Survey reports others' claims and flags the QRAM/oracle dependence; the speedups are not proved here.

papers.partial_detail: 156-page review. Read in full: abstract, contents, Introduction (Sec. 1), Sec. 2.1 to 2.4 and 2.7 (advantage argument, limitations, resource estimates, parallelization), Sec. 5.3, 6.1.3, 6.4, 7.6, 8.7, 8.8 and Sec. 10 Conclusion. Section openings of Sec. 3, 4, 6.2, 8 were skimmed by heading only. Not read: detailed derivations in Sec. 3 to 9 and appendices.
papers.what_it_is: Comprehensive 2022 review of the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE): Hamiltonian encodings, measurement grouping, ansatze, optimizers, error mitigation, resource estimates, and best practices.

assertions.value: The review reports that prior cost studies (noiseless estimates) concluded, under their assumptions, that VQE cannot outperform conventional methods on applications considered tractable.
quotes: They have so far all concluded that given certain assumptions and the current state of research surrounding VQE functionality, the algorithm cannot outperform conventional methods within a remit of applications considered tractable.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors summarize studies by Wecker, Elfving and Gonthier; they also caution that newer measurement methods may change this.

assertions.value: Using stated assumptions (chromium dimer, 52 qubits, 100 ns gates, 10^6 shots, k-UpCCGSD with k=1), the authors estimate that VQE on a single qubit set takes orders of magnitude too long to be viable (Table 2 gives 25 days for one expectation value), which makes parallelization essential.
quotes: it is clear that the time cost of VQE implemented on a single set of qubits remains orders of magnitude too large to be realistically viable, pointing to the dependence of the method on parallelization.
assertions.certainty_reason: Back-of-envelope estimate with optimistic hardware assumptions stated by the authors; the pre-factor is acknowledged as hard to estimate.

assertions.value: The review names four open research areas that decide whether VQE reaches advantage: measurement schemes, large-scale parallelization, vanishing gradients with optimization scaling, and noise and its mitigation.
quotes: optimal measurement schemes for reduction of circuit repetitions required; (2) large scale parallelization across many quantum computers;
ways to overcome the potential appearance of vanishing gradients in the optimization process for large systems
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' stated synthesis of the literature; it is a list of open problems, not a result.

assertions.value: The review states that VQE gradients can vanish exponentially with qubit number (barren plateau) and that it is unclear whether proposed mitigation methods fully contain the problem for VQE.
quotes: gradients of the VQE parameters vanish exponentially with the number of qubits used in the model [86]
Many methods have been proposed to address this problem, but it is currently unclear whether these methods allow one to fully contain the barren plateau problem in the context of VQE
assertions.certainty_reason: Result attributed to cited work (McClean et al.) and a limitation flagged by the authors; not derived in this review.

papers.what_it_is: IBM review-style paper on running the variational quantum eigensolver on near-term devices for chemistry and classical optimization, including a quantum volume metric and error mitigation.

assertions.value: The paper proposes a hardware-neutral quantum volume metric based on qubit count and achievable circuit depth, and argues that adding qubits at constant gate fidelity lowers the metric, so device power grows only if the effective error rate improves too.
quotes: the quantum volume as a metric to compare the power of near-term quantum devices is discussed
which means that a system’s quantum volume decreases if more qubits with the same
when increasing the number of qubits the power of the quantum device will increase only if the
assertions.certainty_reason: Argued from a simple depth ~ 1/(N error) estimate, not a measured result.

assertions.value: The paper states that quantum speedup for classical optimization problems is in many cases modest and, for Ising-type Hamiltonians, unclear because fast classical algorithms exist.
quotes: A more careful analysis shows, however, that the speed-up for classical optimization problems is in many cases rather modest
For Ising-type Hamiltonian problems, it is not clear how much quantum speedup can be expected, because many fast classical algorithms have already been developed
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' assessment citing other work; no new proof or benchmark.

assertions.value: On an ideal (noise-free) simulator, VQE with a heuristic ansatz and no entangler converges to an energy about 50% too high for H2 at equilibrium, while two or more entanglers give the exact energy; for LiH and BeH2, 8 and 28 entangling steps are needed for chemical accuracy without noise. The paper says finite sampling and decoherence cause deviations on current hardware.
quotes: At the equilibrium geometry and no entangler block in the circuit, the energy converges to a state with an energy that is about 50% too high. With two or more entanglers, the exact energy is obtained.

It is demonstrated numerically that in the absence of noise, a number of entangling steps D = 8 and D = 28 are required to achieve chemical accuracy for lithium hydride and beryllium dihydride, respectively, for the given experimental connectivity.
which results in deviations of the simulated bond-dissociation energies from the real values.
assertions.certainty_reason: Noise-free simulation of tiny molecules; the LiH/BeH2 figures are reported from prior work.

assertions.value: A 4-node MaxCut instance solved with a depth-3 heuristic VQE on an ideal simulator after 100 trial steps finds the solution with probability above 95%.
quotes: When we implement this on an ideal quantum simulator [61, 85] and use the VQE to optimize the parameters of the trial state in 100 trial steps, we get the state probabilities shown in Fig. 6(b).
For this simple simulation, the solution is found with a probability that is higher than 95%.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single toy instance on a noise-free simulator; no scaling or hardware evidence.

papers.what_it_is: Xanadu paper defining quantum generative adversarial networks (QuGANs) with a quantum generator and discriminator, quantum-circuit gradient evaluation, and a small numerical demonstration.

assertions.value: The paper defines QuGANs, in which quantum circuits act as generator and discriminator, and gives circuits that evaluate their gradients on a quantum processor, with a classical optimizer updating parameters.
assertions.anchor: Abstract; Sec. II B-C; Conclusion, p. 1, 5-8
quotes: we extend adversarial training to the quantum domain and show how to construct generative adversarial networks using quantum circuits
We have shown how the cost function can be optimized by directly evaluating the gradients with a quantum processor.
assertions.certainty_reason: Method construction with circuit diagrams; validated only by a tiny simulation.

assertions.value: In a numerical test with two labels and pure target states, a QuGAN (42 parameters, 5 qubits) learned a label-conditioned CNOT; the cross-entropy converged to zero. This is a proof of principle, not a performance comparison with classical GANs.
quotes: The expected solution is that G should be able to generate a CNOT gate conditioned on the label register.
With the qubit of register Grad, the algorithm operates on a total of 5 qubits.
As shown in Figure 8, the generator has been properly trained at the end of the algorithm, as the cross-entropy
assertions.certainty_reason: Noise-free simulation of a trivially small task.

assertions.value: The paper states that finding the Nash equilibrium that GAN training targets is a problem known to be in the complexity class PPAD, which is not expected to be contained in BQP.
quotes: This problem is known to be in the complexity class PPAD which is not expected to be contained in BQP [45, 46].
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited complexity statement; 'not expected' is a belief, not a proof.

assertions.value: The authors expect, without proof, that QuGANs will have more versatile representation power than classical GANs, and speculate that a large QuGAN could learn to generate encrypted data labeled by RSA keys since quantum computers can run Shor factoring.
quotes: It is expected that QuGANs will have a more versatile representation power than their classical counterpart.
one can speculate that a large enough QuGAN could learn to generate encrypted data labeled by RSA public encryption keys
assertions.certainty_reason: Explicit speculation; requires fault-tolerant hardware and has no supporting proof or experiment.

papers.what_it_is: Xanadu paper proposing a continuous-variable (photonic) quantum neural network layered circuit with Gaussian affine layers and non-Gaussian nonlinearities, with simulated regression, fraud classification, image generation and autoencoder experiments.

assertions.value: The paper gives a construction that embeds a classical fully connected neural network layer into the CV quantum circuit (Gaussian gates for the affine part, a non-Gaussian gate for the activation) as the special case that creates no superposition or entanglement.
quotes: We show how a classical network can be embedded into the quantum formalism and propose quantum versions of various specialized model such as convolutional, recurrent, and residual networks.
assertions.certainty_reason: Constructive derivation in the paper, but idealised: it uses non-normalizable position eigenstates and a polynomial activation.

assertions.value: The paper argues that CV quantum neural networks are universal for CV quantum computation, and that a modified embedding gives CV-IQP circuits whose exact classical simulation would collapse the polynomial hierarchy (cited result); the approximate case relies on a conjecture. This concerns simulation hardness, not a demonstrated learning advantage.
assertions.anchor: Sec. III C, p. 10-11; Introduction p. 2
quotes: Therefore the full network can also replicate the complete quantum circuit.

This result was extended in Ref. [89] to the case of approximate classical simulation, under the validity of a plausible conjecture concerning the computational complexity of evaluating high-dimensional integrals.
for certain problems, a classical neural network would require exponentially many resources to approximate the quantum network.
assertions.certainty_reason: Hardness rests on cited results and a conjecture, and no task with a learning advantage is shown.

assertions.value: In a classically simulated hybrid classical-quantum classifier on credit card fraud data (284,807 transactions, 0.172% fraudulent), the area under the ROC curve was 0.963; the authors say a classical network could easily outperform it and the model is limited by classical simulation.
quotes: Of the 284, 807 provided transactions, only 0.172% are fraudulent.
an area under the ROC curve of 0.963, compared to the optimal value of 1.

While it is simple to construct a classical neural network to outperform this hybrid model, our network is restricted in both width and depth due to the need to simulate the quantum network on a classical device.
assertions.certainty_reason: Simulated results on one dataset with stated limitation; no hardware and no classical baseline numbers.

assertions.value: In simulated curve fitting of noisy sin, x cubed and sinc functions, fit quality improved with circuit depth up to six layers and then saturated.
quotes: Increasing the number of layers is helpful until a saturation point is reached with six layers, after which little improvement is observed.
assertions.certainty_reason: Single-mode numerical simulation of a 1-D toy regression task with a truncated Hilbert space.

papers.what_it_is: 2023 review of quantum algorithms for finance (JPMorgan Chase and collaborators) covering stochastic modeling, optimization and machine learning, with assessment of caveats.

assertions.value: The review states that quantum-native models (QNNs, quantum circuit Born machines, quantum kernels) may be classically intractable to simulate but it is unclear whether they give advantage on classical problems; advantage is shown only for data from quantum processes and early numerics do not extend to classical problems.
quotes: Quantum-native models, such as quantum neural networks, quantum circuit Born machine and quantum kernel methods, circumvent the issues of QBLASs and can be intractable to classically simulate, however, it is currently unclear if they provide advantage on classical problems.
initial numerical evidence suggests this does not extend to classical problems
Whereas at the moment, quantum advantage on classical problems by using quantum-native methods appears to be unlikely
this has only been shown to provide advantage for problems involving data generated from quantum processes
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' literature assessment citing other papers; no new experiment.

assertions.value: The review states that QBLAS-based quantum ML speedups mostly assume quantum memory (the review says it is unclear whether such a device can be built) and some give speedups only for low-rank data, where the speedup is not exponential.
quotes: most of these algorithms work in a setting with quantum memory
It is currently unclear if such a device can be constructed.
Furthermore, a variety of these approaches only provide speedups when the data has low-rank approximations, and in this setting, the speedup is not exponential as it was once thought.
assertions.certainty_reason: Reviewer's summary of the QRAM and dequantization literature.

assertions.value: The review states that dequantization yields classical randomized algorithms with dimension dependence competitive with the best quantum algorithm when given sampling access to a data structure holding low-rank data.
quotes: Dequantization results in a classical randomized algorithm that achieves a dimension dependence that is competitive with the best quantum algorithm when provided sampling access to a certain data structure containing low-rank data.
assertions.certainty_reason: Standard result attributed to Tang and follow-up work, summarized correctly by the reviewers.

assertions.value: The conclusion says provable quantum advantages exist in black-box settings such as Monte Carlo integration, but it is unclear whether any proposed approach for stochastic modeling, optimization or ML gives an end-to-end advantage on practical problems.
quotes: Promising provable quantum advantages have been discovered in certain black-box settings, such as MCI.
it is still unclear whether any of these proposed approaches for stochastic modeling, optimization and ML can be turned into an end-to-end quantum advantage on practical problems.
assertions.certainty_reason: Authors' summary of the state of the field as of 2023; depends on data loading, readout and fault tolerance.
